title.narrative: Harare Sustainable City Initiative: Promotion of Carbon-Neutral Urban Basic Services And Energy Efficient Built Environment.

description.narrative: The project aims at enhancing the overall wellbeing, health and security conditions of Zimbabwe citizens and particularly those living in informal settlements, through access to better urban basic services from sustainable solid waste management and the use of renewable energy systems; the project will also create systems for access to affordable carbon-neutral building materials. This will be achieved through improved operations of municipal solid waste management, energy and resource recovery, renewable energy generation and promotion of climate responsive building material production. The project will enhance energy access of targeted communities by providing reliable and renewable energy supply generated from locally available resources. According to UN-Habitat’s SDG indicator 11.6.1 survey in 2021, 40 only 25% of total municipal solid waste generated in Harare are collected and 2% is managed in controlled facilities 27% is much lower than average of Sub-Saharan Africa. Lack of service coverage and low efficiency of waste collection services is due to ageing, dilapidated and overused equipment + infrastructure, frequent breakdowns of collection vehicles due to lack of maintenance (O & M), overreliance on hired equipment and contracting, operating environment characterized by hyperinflation, political interference, and weak public financial management system. Zimbabwe has less than 50% of electricity access, and urban and peri-urban poor have limited access to reliable energy sources. Zimbabwe is experiencing an unprecedented disparity between the supply and demand of electricity. While the total demand for electricity is 2029 MW, the supply is only around 1200 MW. The grid has notable carbon footprint as the main share of final electricity consumption comes from fossil-based sources such as diesel generators running during the power outages and others that contribute to the grid electricity generation mix. A 2021 report on financing public infrastructure in Zimbabwe claimed that Zimbabwe requires USD 2 billion annually until 2032 for financing economic infrastructure (Kapesa et al). Complemented by the fact that Zimbabwe has a huge national housing backlog estimated at 1,25 million housing units countrywide, the potential energy and resource inefficiencies in closing this infrastructure gap using traditional building methods and resources may have huge negative ramifications on the environmental sustainability landscape of the country, and of the world at large. Zimbabwe is a signatory to the Habitat Agenda and subscribes to the principle of improving the standards of human settlement for its populace. Therefore, it is imperative that the country fosters energy and resource efficiencies in the built environment for a better urban future for all. The project adopts an integrated approach to the energy deficit in Harare and has identified 3 critical sectors that together can significantly improve energy availability through resource recovery, renewable energy production and the reduction of energy demand in the building sector. It addresses these interventions by developing situation analysis, promoting innovative technologies and solutions and building around them governance and business activities involving marginalized groups and focusing on disadvantaged areas, while providing city-wide solutions. The city of Harare lacks the resources and capacities for effective Municipal Solid Waste Management (MSWM). This results in extremely low waste collection rate and even when it is collected, they are disposed in an open dumpsite (Pomona). This approach only spatially displaces the waste, often outside the city into rural areas, contribute to soil and water pollutions, aggravates greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and increases the difficulty of final treatment of waste and material recovery. Currently 41 tonnes per day, 5% of total municipal solid waste generation is being recovered in Harare, compared to its potential of recoverable amount of 535 tonnes per day. Turning the current linear approach into more circular approach harnessing the recyclables generated daily in Harare has a huge potential to reduce pollution, mitigate greenhouse gas emission, improve public health and create decent green jobs.The project intends to strengthen ongoing attempts of zero waste approaches by improving the working conditions of people and institutions involved in energy and material recovery from wastes. The project also intends to utilize the generated wastes for energy generation and recycle these materials adding value for their reuse. The project will build on the UN-Habitat’s past effort on baselining of SDG indicator 11.6.1 survey conducted under African Clean Cities Platform, at the same time taking stock of current situation of energy access, energy efficiency in building and building material production with a particular attention on their impact on the environment and their carbon footprint.
